title: Critique that states high standards
statement: Open critical feedback on a learner's work with a fixed line saying the standard is high and they can reach it, then give specific critique, not praise padding.
example: In randomized field trials, 71% of African American students revised an essay returned with such a note, against 17% with a neutral note.
detail: The Grade 9 research brief read the wise-feedback trials in full: essays returned with a note stating very high expectations and confidence that the student could reach them were revised far more often, 71% against 17% with a neutral note among African American students (covariate-adjusted) and 87% against 62% among White students, and a third study, in a high school, raised African American students' grades. The brief makes it a rule for the lesson's AI marker: every critique opens with a fixed sentence stating high standards and confidence in the student, then gives specific, critical feedback, not praise padding such as 'Great try!' before a hint.
against: The trials were randomized field trials, mostly in grade 7, with one in a high school (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, lines 23 and 25); the fixed sentence has not been tried in critiques a model writes.

evidence.quote: Among African American students, 71% revised with this note versus 17% with a neutral note (covariate-adjusted).
Every critique the LLM rubric returns should open with a fixed sentence stating high standards and confidence in the student.
It should give specific, critical feedback, not praise padding.
